s1.p1: In this section we will learn about logical values, logical variables, logical expressions and logical operators.
s2.p1: When a person declares that his son is 18 years old, that statement will be true for one year, but before that year and after that year, that statement will be a lie. And that is on the condition that this person has a son.
s2.p2: Suppose a man wrote this statement on his social media page when he was 15 years old.
s2.p3: He did not yet have a son, and the statement was false.
s2.p4: Then he grew up, got married and had a son, but the statement remained false because his son was not yet 18.
s2.p5: Finally, when his son turned 18, the statement became true.
s2.p6: But it lasted for one year.
s2.p7: Then his son turned 19, and this statement became false again.
s2.p8: Thus, this statement is a **variable**. For its meaning can change.
s2.p9: The values this variable can take are **⟦f0⟧** or **⟦f1⟧**
s2.p12: ![ico-25 warn] **There are no other logical values.
s2.p13: ^^We don't have such a sly value as ‘Not everything is so unambiguous’. Everything is unambiguous. It's either black or white. Our world is simple.^^
s2.p14: So, our variable can take one of two possible logical values (**⟦f4⟧** or **⟦f5⟧**).
s3.p1: The statement '_The apple is red and round_' can be decomposed into two parts: '_Apple is red_' + '_Apple is round_'.
s3.p2: I.e. we are actually dealing with two logical variables, each of which takes a logical value, i.e. is a variable of logical type.
s3.p4: Let the boolean variable **⟦f7⟧** take the value **⟦f8⟧** when the property **⟦f9⟧** has the value ‘red’ and the boolean variable **⟦f10⟧** take the value **⟦f11⟧** when the property **⟦f12⟧** has the value ‘round’.
s3.p5: The **⟦f13⟧** variable takes the value **⟦f14⟧** when the variable **⟦f15⟧** has the value **⟦f16⟧** and the  variable **⟦f17⟧** has the value **⟦f18⟧**, too.
s3.p11: Then the variable **⟦f31⟧** is already a **logical expression**, because it requires its value to be calculated based on the values of the variables **⟦f32⟧** and **⟦f33⟧**.
s3.p12: And this logical expression will have the value **⟦f34⟧** only when both variables **⟦f35⟧** and **⟦f36⟧** have the value **⟦f37⟧**.
s3.p13: A **Logical Expression** is an expression whose evaluation will result in a logical value.
s3.p14: The simplest case of a logical expression is a logical value.
s3.p15: Let's see how we can construct more complex logical expressions.
s4.p1: The simplest way to construct logical expressions is to use **comparison operators**.
s4.p2: These are binary operators, meaning they have two operands.
s4.p3: The operands can be variables or expressions.
s4.p4: ![ico-25 warn] Comparison operators compare not only the **values** but also the **data types** of the operands.
s4.p5: Comparison operators always return a **logical value**.
s4.p7: | **⟦f38⟧**  | non-strict equality ^^(only operand values are compared, under the bonnet, data types are converted)^^ |
s4.p8: | **⟦f39⟧** | strict equality ^^(operand data types are compared, and if the operand data type is the same, the operand values are compared)^^ |
s4.p9: | **⟦f40⟧**  | non-strict inequality ^^(values are not equal, data type is ignored)^^ |
s4.p10: | **⟦f41⟧** | strict inequality ^^(will return ⟦f42⟧ if the data types or values are not equal)^^ |
s4.p16: Each character has a numeric code, and the character codes are compared.
s4.p17: If the first characters of the string operands are equal, the next characters are compared, and so on until the code of the characters will be different.

s6.p1: There are three logical operators in JS: **logical multiplication**, **logical addition** and **logical negation**.
s6.p2: The **logical negation** operator is a unary operator, meaning it has only one operand.
s6.p3: The logical operators of multiplication and addition are binary operators, they have two operands.
s6.p4: Logical negation always returns a logical value, even if the operand is not a logical expression (or logical value).
s6.p5: The **logical multiplication**, **logical addition** operators do not always return a logical value.
s6.p6: When performing logical operations under the bonnet, the engine casts the operands to the **⟦f47⟧** data type.
s6.p8: Since type conversion to type **⟦f49⟧** is fairly straightforward, we can ‘get ahead of ourselves’ a bit:
s6.p9: 1. An empty string is cast to **⟦f50⟧**. If the length of the string is greater than 0, such a string will be cast to **⟦f51⟧** no matter what characters are in that string.
s6.p10: 2. Numbers other than 0 and **⟦f52⟧** are cast to **⟦f53⟧**, and 0 and **⟦f54⟧** are cast to **⟦f55⟧**.
s6.p12: 4. Any data structures (arrays, objects) are always cast to **⟦f59⟧**, regardless of the contents of those data structures or the complete lack of contents.

s8.p4: In the following examples, we use the logical operator **⟦f68⟧** to operands that are **logical expressions**.
s8.p5: We construct logical expressions using comparison operators.
s8.p10: However, this is JS, and we can apply logical operators to data of any type.
s8.p11: In this case, [►►►**implicit type conversion**►►►](⟦f70⟧) starts working, i.e. operands are cast to a logical type, and then the value of the expression is calculated as follows: if the logical value after casting the first operand to a logical data type is ⟦f69⟧, then the value of the first operand is returned, otherwise the value of the second operand is returned.
s8.p13: Note the fact that the use of the logical operator **⟦f71⟧** does not uniquely determine the type of the result.
s8.p14: The data type of the value that will be obtained by the engine as a result of evaluating the expression depends on the data type of the operands.
s9.p6: So, logical addition works according to the principle: if after casting to the data type **⟦f73⟧** **at least one of the operands** is **⟦f74⟧**, the whole expression will have the value **⟦f75⟧**. Since the values of the other operands will no longer change the result, the engine stops at the first operand that will yield **⟦f76⟧** after type conversion. However, the **⟦f77⟧** operator returns not **⟦f78⟧**, but the original value of the operand.
